summary:
Sejong stands under the national framework of South Korea, which does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and where consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sources record no Sejong-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding touching trans people, so what a visitor faces is the national legal position as interpreted by the courts. That position is documented and enforceable rather than nominal.

Legal gender recognition no longer requires surgery. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to condition a gender change on surgery and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are now reference material rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity.

Trans visitors hold a judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 22 July 2024 a Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, ruling that police advice to a person transitioning from male to female, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights. The appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right.

Protections outside these two areas are thin. South Korea has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on those grounds, and there is no same-sex marriage for a visitor travelling with a partner, although the Constitutional Court did extend recognition to same-sex partners' healthcare rights in a 2024 ruling. Organised conservative opposition remains active, and Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in the country.

No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.
tangentialFactors:
The 2021 survey by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% avoided facilities out of fear, indicating that the enforceable restroom right coexists with practical avoidance shaped by anticipated hostility rather than by law.

The restroom claimant had already secured a family-register gender change in 2020, so the police advice was issued to a person whose legal sex was settled; the ruling constrains official conduct toward people whose documents are already amended as well as those in transition.

Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report pairs its findings on discrimination against LGBT people with a relatively positive overall assessment of free media and civil society in the country, which bears on how readily a visitor can seek assistance or publicity if something goes wrong.

Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are described as broadly positive environments, a contrast with the national absence of anti-discrimination legislation.
localsOnly:
Residents may change their registered sex without sex-reassignment surgery following the 8 May 2024 Yeongdong ruling, which reduced prior judicial guidelines requiring surgery to reference status rather than a test applied to applicants.

The Supreme Court has allowed a transgender person with minor children to change their gender in the family relations register, so parenthood does not by itself block recognition.

Transgender people are excluded from military service in South Korea, while Military Criminal Act article 92-6 exposes military personnel to up to two years' imprisonment for consensual same-sex conduct; the Constitutional Court upheld that provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination in employment, services or accommodation on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and there is no same-sex marriage.

In healthcare, the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request in November 2023 to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, stating that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult; the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged this as a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the concentration of national government agencies in Sejong changes the official climate for trans residents or visitors is not documented in these sources; the inventory contains no Sejong-specific enforcement, facility or incident record.

Entry, visa and border-screening treatment of trans documents is not sourced here, including whether passport or entry-record markers are checked against legal sex status.

The sources do not establish how the Yeongdong and Seoul rulings are applied by lower courts outside those districts, or whether administrative agencies have issued implementing instructions on surgery-free recognition.

The material on organised conservative opposition describes general activity and does not identify a specific trans-directed incident with date or outcome.
